_audit: FACT + SPOILER audit of the thirteen post-trim narration lines (ids 11, 22, 24, 36, 39, 43, 54, 60, 64, 77, 80, 86, 108). Current text read from draft.json. PRE-TRIM text read from narration_fit_todo.json, which is the actual input to this trim round - NOT draft_prefit.json, which is an older stage (it predates the trim round audited in fact_audit_trims.json and differs from the todo text on lines 36, 39, 43, 64, 77, 80, 86, 108). Trimmer claims in narration_fit_done.json treated as unverified and checked one by one. Authorities: beats_proposal.md (beat map B01-B109 + reveal-map), film_facts.json, names.json, transcript.json (559 segments, timestamps cited), shots.json (shot-level on-screen descriptions, used only for on-screen appearance/action facts), reveals.json.
_trimmer_claim_check: All thirteen 'dropped' claims in narration_fit_done.json were compared against narration_fit_todo.json and all thirteen are ACCURATE. (An earlier pass of this audit against draft_prefit.json appeared to show the trimmer under-reporting large rewrites on lines 36, 80, 86 and 108; that was an artefact of using the wrong baseline. draft_prefit.json is two stages back.) Two justifications are nevertheless wrong on the merits - line 64 ('the beat map does not mention the white suit' - true, but shots.json verifies it, and the beat map does not mention the panama hat the trimmer kept either) and line 43 ('the walk-back was a flourish, not a fact' - shots.json clip:00:46:10 shows exactly that walk-past-and-turn-back). Neither wrong justification produced a wrong line.

lines.fact: ok - every clause matched to footage. 'muscle car launches off the dirt and tumbles end over end' = shots.json clip:00:09:07 verbatim ('a pale muscle car launches off the dirt and tumbles end over end'); 'lands upside down' = clip:00:09:26 ('settles upside down in the dust'); 'Sean hanging in his belt, bloody' = clip:00:09:26 ('a body hanging inverted in its belt, then pushes to a face smeared with blood'); 'both cars wrecked' = clip:00:09:16 ('the two wrecks grinding together') + B08 ('The cars collide'); 'a crowd full of cameras' = clip:00:09:07 ('races past desert spectators; a bystander films from an SUV window') + B09 ('the bystander video of the race'). B08 attributes the tumble to the collision rather than to the dirt launch; the collision is carried one line earlier by line 10 ('The two cars touch at speed'), so no causal claim is broken.
lines.fact_loss: none - the trim was punctuation only (em dash to full stop, to stop the dash costing a token under len(text.split())). Pre-trim text in narration_fit_todo.json is word-identical.
lines.spoiler: ok - no R1/R2/R3/R4 held term; B08 is at 00:09:07, far ahead of every reveal.
lines.payload: ok - payload=stake, and the stake (both cars destroyed, on camera, in front of witnesses) is what sets up the strike-three beat at line 13.
lines.notes: The only cost is a sentence fragment ('Both cars wrecked in front of a crowd full of cameras.') where there used to be an appositive. Meaning unchanged. Cleanest of the thirteen.

lines.beat: B28 (per draft note; content is actually B27)
lines.fact: FAIL on one clause. 'rises' ok (B27: 'rises from his seat'; shots.json clip:00:23:56: 'rises glowering'). 'collecting cash and phones' ok (B27: 'taking cash and phones'; clip:00:23:56: 'cash and phones in hand'). 'The garage answers to him' ok - lifted verbatim from B27. Both sources say he moves THROUGH the meet - B27 'moves through the meet with his crew', clip:00:23:56 'moving through the meet'. With 'the meet' as a bare direct object the dominant English reading of 'moves the meet' is that he RELOCATES the gathering, which nothing in the film, the beat map or the shot list supports. Pre-existing (the same wording is in narration_fit_todo.json), not introduced by this trim, but it is wrong as the line now stands.
lines.fact_loss: none caused by the trim. The dropped word was the colour adjective 'black' ('black leather' -> 'leather'). B27 and clip:00:23:56 both say black leather jacket, so a verified detail did leave the script, but it is not load-bearing: the spiky hair plus the leather still match the man on screen in this line's own clip window (00:24:27-00:24:34, where clip:00:24:27 has 'the leather-jacket man and his crew fronting them'), and line 23 names him Takashi one line later.
lines.invention: none introduced by this trim - 'moves the meet' predates it.
lines.spoiler: ok - the deliberate withholding of the name for one line is a staging choice, not a reveal breach; no R1/R2/R3/R4 term appears. 'The garage answers to him' does not touch R3.
lines.payload: ok - payload=stake; the authority beat survives intact and is the point of the line.
lines.notes: Second, separate problem: the draft's note field says B28, but the content is B27 (00:23:56, the rise and the collection). B28 (00:24:27) is the gaijin confrontation, and line 23 already carries B28. So B27 has no line pointing at it and line 22 is mis-noted - which is also why its clip window (00:24:27-00:24:34) is B28 footage while its words describe action that finished 30 seconds earlier. Pre-existing in narration_fit_todo.json (beat: B28). Worth fixing upstream; it is not a trim defect.

lines.fact: FAIL on who performs the action. Supported: 'Twinkie spells it out: that man is Yakuza' - transcript 1503.36, 'Hey, yo, look, man, it's Yakuza', spoken by the friend in the red beanie per B29 ('His friend warns him that the man is Yakuza'), confirmed again at 1532.68/1533.68 ('You know Yakuza? / The mafia?'). Supported: 'He calls him out' - clip:00:25:47, 'The American calls out across the floor'; B29, 'he calls him out across the floor anyway'. UNSUPPORTED: 'stops an inch from his face' with Sean as the subject. Both sources put the advance on Takashi, not Sean: clip:00:25:47 'the spiky-haired man breaks away from her and pushes through the crowd toward him'; clip:00:25:53 'the spiky-haired man closes on the American until the two are squared off nose to nose... neither backing off'; B29 'the man squares up nose to nose and takes the bait'. The line makes Sean the one who crosses the distance. The end state (an inch apart) is right; the agency is reversed.
lines.fact_loss: none - the only change was 'He calls the man out' -> 'He calls him out' (one word).
lines.attribution: 'Twinkie spells it out' present - the Yakuza claim stays Twinkie's, exactly as in the pre-trim text. The narrator does not assert it. PASS on this check.
lines.spoiler: ok - 'Yakuza' on its own is not an R1 held term (R1 holds 'robbing the Yakuza' and 'stealing from the Yakuza'); no R2/R3/R4 term.
lines.payload: ok - payload=stake, and the loop into line 25 ('Let's race.') still fires.
lines.notes: Referent check requested by the brief: 'the man' -> 'him' is CLEAN. 'that man is Yakuza' sits eight words earlier in the same line and is the only available antecedent once 'He' is fixed as Sean by 'Sean takes it as a dare'. No ambiguity introduced. Second doubt, not failed: 'and two words close it' sits inside a sentence whose subject is Sean, so a listener will hear the two words as Sean's, but B29 attributes 'let's race' to the MAN ('the man squares up nose to nose and takes the bait: let's race'). The clause is grammatically agentless so it does not assert a speaker, and line 25 delivers the quote as film-speak - but if line 25 is heard as Sean's, that is wrong per B29. Also: the exact two words are NOT FOUND in the transcript - the nearest segments are 1502.36 'Come on, man, let's rock' and 1536.95 'Hey D. Let's go. It's time a race' (ASR garble). 'Let's race' is beat-map supported (B29) only.

However that shot runs 00:46:10-00:46:20 and this line's window starts at 00:46:20, so the walk-back is no longer on screen while the words play. 'Eyes a red Evo' matches what IS on screen. lines.fact: ok, and the quote is verified from the shot list rather than the transcript. The on-screen text is NOT FOUND in transcript.json (it is typed, not spoken - a fuzzy scan for 'bama' and 'never c u' returns nothing). It IS verified verbatim in shots.json clip:00:58:29, this line's own clip window: 'the dark-haired girl in the school uniform works at a laptop showing a Japanese text document; a chat window cuts in over it reading bama_boy: how come i never c u drift??? and she reads it'. 'That night they eat vending-machine food under an overpass' = clip:00:58:45, 'Night: a wide of a parking lot under a stacked highway overpass, then inserts of vending machines... before the camera finds the two of them eating together at a table', and B64, 'they end up eating vending-machine food together under the overpass'.
lines.fact_loss: none. 'A chat window' was dropped (29 -> 26 words) but nothing else, and the chat window is physically on screen in clip:00:58:29 while the words play.
lines.attribution: the message stays attributed to Neela by 'On Neela's laptop:' - and B64 is explicit that she is the sender ('The dark-haired schoolgirl messages him from class asking why she never sees him drift'), as is clip:00:58:37 ('Hands type on the laptop keyboard and she breaks into a private smile; a finger hits Enter and the cut lands on the American boy at his own laptop... reading the same chat line').
lines.payload: ok - payload=rest; the relationship turn ('the guard drops away') is the function and it survives.
lines.notes: Three doubts, none fatal. (1) The brief's question - does a viewer still know it is an on-screen message? YES: 'On Neela's laptop:' plus a colon plus unpunctuated lowercase text-speak, over footage in which the chat window literally cuts in over her screen. The meaning does not rest on typography alone; it rests on typography plus the shot. (2) 'bama_boy:' is formatted on screen like a SENDER handle, and 'bama' is Sean's (Alabama). Read that way the message would be HIS, and the narration would have flipped the author. B64 and the type-then-Enter-then-he-reads-it shot order both say she is the sender, so the narration is right - but the on-screen string on its own is genuinely ambiguous. (3) 'the guard drops away' is placed on B64, whereas the beat map puts that phrase on B66 ('the guard between them drops into laughter', 01:00:28, the mountain drive). Line 57 covers B66 and does NOT restate it, so there is no duplication, and the overpass dialogue in the transcript (3534.9-3551.17, 'It's actually not bad... I'm not a cool guy... It's what they used to call me when I was a kid / I thought you were born here') supports the guard dropping here. Placement is defensible, not sourced.

lines.attribution: 'says' kept, so the three words stay hers; the quote itself lands on line 61 ('You've changed, DK.'), verified at transcript 3841.72.

lines.fact: ok on all four claims. (a) 'the panama hat belongs to Kamata' = shots.json clip:01:06:27, 'An older man in a white suit and panama hat appears in the yellow corridor... by the last shot Kamata has stepped into the back room greeted as the uncle he was about to visit' (chars: Kamata), corroborated by clip:01:07:09's blue-lit-office description of 'an elderly man in a white suit and panama hat sunk in a leather armchair'. (b) 'the uncle DK answers to' = film_facts.json ('Kamata / Takashi's uncle, the head of the yakuza'), B89 ('naming the rival as Kamata's nephew'), B90 (Takashi bows to him), names.json (Takashi = DK). (c) 'Takashi hands over the week's take' = B72, 'Kamata collects last week's take from the man in the black shirt', and clip:01:06:39 (this line's window), 'the talk turns to business as he leans over the desk and hands across last week's take, Kamata standing over him'. (d) 'Kamata sits down to the books' = B72, 'sits down at the desk to go through the books', and clip:01:06:59, 'the wide finds the old man at the desk with a ledger open, working through the books'.
lines.fact_loss: 'white suit' left the script. It was a VERIFIED fact, not an unverified one - shots.json clip:01:06:27 and clip:01:07:09 both state it, and the previous round's audit (fact_audit_trims.json) had already passed it on exactly that evidence. It now appears nowhere in draft.json. Not reported as a FAIL because it is a non-load-bearing costume detail whose only job was appearance-ID, and the panama hat, verified in the same two shots, still does that job.
lines.invention: none. 'the old man sits down to the books' -> 'Kamata sits down to the books' only resolves a pronoun to a name already established at line 39.
lines.spoiler: ok, and this is the tightest spoiler margin in the set. B72 is at 01:06:39 and R1 lands at 01:07:29 - fifty seconds later. 'sits down to the books' is beat-map wording ('go through the books') and is NOT the R1 held term 'cooking the books'; it describes a man auditing his own ledgers, which is the setup, not the reveal. No R1 term ('the missing money', 'where the money went', 'a thief', 'siphoning') appears. Clean.
lines.payload: ok - payload=rest; the line's job is to put Kamata, the hierarchy and the ledger on the table so that line 66 (B73) can land the accusation. All three present.
lines.notes: Direct answer to the brief's question: the beat map does NOT mention the white suit, so the trimmer's premise is factually true - but the inference drawn from it is wrong twice over. First, the beat map does not mention the panama hat either, so the stated test would have deleted the detail the trimmer chose to keep. Second, the right authority for an on-screen appearance fact is shots.json, which verifies both. So: the beat map does not CONTRADICT the white suit, the ORIGINAL was correct, and the removal was unnecessary but harmless. Minor: the hat/suit are described in clip:01:06:27, one shot BEFORE this line's window (01:06:39-01:06:48), where Kamata is 'standing over him' at the desk - same scene, same costume, so the identification still works, but the hat is being named over footage that the shot list does not describe it in.

lines.fact: every surviving claim is supported. 'Dark lane' = B81, 'waiting in the dark lane at the house', and shots.json clip:01:16:30, 'stand in a dark alley'. 'Takashi's pistol at Sean's head' = B81, 'gets a pistol to the young American's head', and clip:01:16:42, 'the scuffle ends with the henley man levelling a pistol'; the henley man is Takashi - B82 has the young woman go with him (Neela goes with her boyfriend, not with Morimoto), and the same black-shirt/black-henley figure runs B75, B76, B80 and clip:01:06:39. 'his father draws' = B81, 'the older man in the olive jacket draws on him in return', and clip:01:16:42, 'an older man aims one back at him'; that the older man is SEAN's father is confirmed by B83, 'the older man claims the mess as his responsibility as the boy's father'. The causal 'until' is supported by B81's 'in return'.
lines.fact_loss: FAIL - and this is the reason for the verdict. The dropped verb is 'waits', and B81 states it explicitly: 'The man in the black henley IS WAITING in the dark lane at the house'. shots.json clip:01:16:30 states it too: 'a shadow moves at a parked car, and the man in the black henley emerges from the dark'. That is premeditation - Takashi did not run into Sean, he came to Sean's home and lay in wait for him - and it is a fact, not a nuance of posture. It is now absent from the entire script: line 76 (B80) ends with Takashi driving away from the crash, line 78 (B82) covers Neela breaking the standoff, line 79 (B83) is the father in the alley. None of them says he was lying in wait. Also absent script-wide, though never in this line even pre-trim: 'at the house' - B81 places the ambush at Sean's home, which is what makes it an escalation rather than a street encounter.
lines.invention: none. 'pistol to Sean's head' -> 'pistol at Sean's head' is identical.
lines.spoiler: ok - B81 is at 01:16:30, after R2 landed at 01:15:07, so there is nothing left to protect here; no R3 or R4 term appears.
lines.payload: weakened but not destroyed - payload=stake, and the gun at Sean's head is still the stake. What is gone is the agency behind it: 'Dark lane: Takashi's pistol at Sean's head' is a tableau, where 'Takashi waits... ' was an act.
lines.notes: Direct answer to the brief's question - losing 'waits' loses a FACT, not only a nuance, because B81 and clip:01:16:30 both assert the waiting and nothing else in the script carries it. Also noted: 'until his father draws' is referentially ambiguous between Takashi's father and Sean's (Takashi's uncle, not his father, has been established at lines 39 and 64, and Sean is the nearer antecedent, so it resolves correctly - but it resolves by inference). This ambiguity is pre-existing and the suggested fix does not make it worse. Separately: the draft note is now B81, which matches the content; narration_fit_todo.json also says B81, but the clip window (01:16:58-01:17:02) is B82 footage (clip:01:16:58, 'the pistol stays locked at the young man's head' - the drawing already happened at 01:16:42). So the words describe B81 over B82 pictures. Pre-existing mapping issue, not a trim defect.

lines.fact: ok on the sourced claims. 'he tells Twinkie he is walking into Kamata's house himself' = B86, 'The American decides to walk into Kamata's place and settle it himself', and B85/clip:01:19:18 for the argument with the friend. 'Twinkie calls it suicide' = B86 verbatim, 'his friend calls it suicide'. Twinkie is the friend: film_facts.json ('Bow Wow / Twinkie / the first friend Sean meets in Tokyo'), and the B85-B87 run is the cornrowed/mint-green friend who also owns the green minivan (line 82, B87). The opening judgment 'That's the first time in his life he refuses to be moved on' is an inference, not a sourced fact - see notes.
lines.fact_loss: none. The only change against narration_fit_todo.json is 'That is' -> "That's" (29 -> 28 words). The trimmer's claim is accurate.
lines.attribution: both attributions PRESENT and verified against the pre-trim text: 'he tells Twinkie' and 'Twinkie calls it suicide'. The narrator does not assert that the plan is suicidal in its own voice - that judgment stays Twinkie's, which is the correct handling and the specific failure mode this project has hit twice before.
lines.invention: none introduced by this trim. 'That is the first time in his life he refuses to be moved on' is present word for word in narration_fit_todo.json, so it was not manufactured by the shortening.
lines.spoiler: ok - no held term. B86 is at 01:19:18; R3 lands at 01:33:41 and nothing here anticipates it.
lines.payload: ok - payload=loop, and the loop still fires. The line now ends on Twinkie's challenge ('Twinkie calls it suicide'), and line 81 is the film-speak answer 'That's all I've got.' - which is B86's own ending ('he answers that it is all he has left'). The handover is implicit rather than teased, but it lands.
lines.notes: One standing doubt, pre-existing rather than trim-caused. 'the first time in his life' is an unverifiable superlative. It is consistent with the established record - B46/line 38 (army brat, moved around), B13 (his mother tells him they are not moving this time), B17 (he cannot keep moving away from his own trouble), B84 (his father presses him to get out of Tokyo and he walks off without answering) - so it is a narrator judgment built on sourced facts, which is permitted. But it also pre-empts the closing thesis: line 109 says 'Sean spent his whole life being moved on - new town, new school, new nobody - and he only wins the day he stops running'. Saying it first at line 80 spends the ending's punch 29 lines early. A craft call, not a fact failure, so not scored as one.

lines.fact: ok on all four claims, matched clause for clause against B90 ('The nephew protests at being silenced and Kamata, without a word, stares him down until he drops into a bow'). 'Kamata says nothing' = 'without a word'. 'He just stares' = 'stares him down'. "Takashi's defiance folds into a bow" = 'The nephew protests... until he drops into a bow', with Takashi identified as the nephew by film_facts.json and B89. The protest itself is carried by line 85 ('Takashi throws it back - after everything you've done, you're giving me orders? Kamata just lets him hang himself'), so the 'defiance' this line folds has already been shown.

The trimmer's claim is accurate against narration_fit_todo.json. (Against the older draft_prefit.json a whole sentence is missing - 'One look does what no shouting could.' - but that was removed in a previous round, not this one.)
lines.attribution: n/a (no reported speech) - and worth stating positively: the line reports silence, so there is no motive to mis-assert. 'Kamata says nothing. He just stares' describes behaviour only; it does not claim to know what Kamata thinks.
lines.spoiler: ok - B90 is at 01:22:50, after R1 and R2 and before R3; no R3 term ('inherits the throne', 'takes DK's place') or R4 term appears. 'Kamata is the only still thing in a film about motion' is a judgment about staging, not about outcome.
lines.payload: ok - payload=judgment, and the judgment that is the line's whole reason for existing survives verbatim.
lines.notes: Nothing marginal. Cleanest judgment line of the thirteen.

lines.fact: three of the four required claims verify hard; the fourth rests on reveals.json alone. (1) AMERICAN MUSCLE - PRESENT and verified: B108, 'a bald man in a white tee in a hulking American muscle car'; shots.json clip:01:36:38 (this line's window), 'His green coupe noses up beside a hulking American muscle car with the crowd banked behind them; the camera pushes in on the rival machine and reveals its driver'. The contrast 'no tuner coupe' is right - Sean's own car is the green coupe. (2) DOMINIC TORETTO - PRESENT; the driver is a bald man in a white tee (B108, clip:01:36:38) and reveals.json R4 names him: 'the challenger who turns up for the closing race is Dominic Toretto'. A scan for 'famil' over all 559 segments returns exactly two hits - 2449.02 ('And now you're fanning your family with these drift nuts', a different scene) and 5757.43 ('and how I was family'). 5757.43 falls at 01:35:57, inside clip:01:35:49, which is B107 - the green-jacketed man (Twinkie) calling out the man in the black tee - and line 107 ALREADY uses that utterance. So the claim that TORETTO says Han was family to him is supported by reveals.json R4 and by nothing else. Mitigating: the ASR is demonstrably lossy here - three segments for the final four minutes, across two spoken scenes - and shots.json clip:01:36:46 confirms a two-way conversation exists ('The two drivers talk across the lane through their open windows'). reveals.json is a listed authority and states it explicitly, so I pass it, but this is the weakest-evidenced assertion in the thirteen and it should be eyeballed against the footage before ship. Second, smaller note: 'Toretto grins' - clip:01:36:46 says 'the bald man is laughing and the young driver is grinning back', i.e. the grin is Sean's and the laugh is Toretto's. Laughing entails a grin, so this is not wrong, but the source puts the word on the other man.
